newsitem.title: USA: Big acre turnover for U.S land, water plan.
newsitem.headline: Big acre turnover for U.S land, water plan.

text.p: The nation's largest land and water conservation program will set aside 16 million acres of farm land this fall -- about the size of West Virginia -- and deliver more environmental benefits at lower cost, Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said Thursday.
"This is probably the most important environmental program in government," Glickman told a news conference.
The Conservation Reserve, which pays farmers to idle fragile land for 10 years, was created in 1985. The reserve's goal is to reduce erosion, protect water quality and improve wildlife habitat.
In its early days, the reserve's purpose was to limit farm output as well as conservation, but those days are gone, Glickman said.
"A higher (acreage) number at this time would have retired more productive land and a lower number would have missed out on some tremendous conservation opportunities," he said.
Environmentalists praised the new focus of the reserve. The Environmental Working Group said the 16.1 million acres were the largest amount ever set aside.

Grain and food industry groups had advocated a smaller enrollment, perhaps 12 million acres or so, on the grounds it was foolish to lock away land when food demand was booming. They expressed mild disappointment with Glickman's decision.

Senate Agriculture Committee Chairman Richard Lugar, Indiana Republican, applauded the "more environmentally targeted and economical" reserve, but cautioned the government against idling so much land that food production suffered.

Because enrollment is smaller than the 21.2 million acres coming out of the program, about five million acres will be freed for crops and livestock. Farmers will be given another chance this fall to offer land for the reserve.

To underline the tighter focus of the program, the Agriculture Department said 13.5 million acres of the new enrollment was considered at high risk of erosion and 5.5 million acres were in high-priority water quality regions.

Sen. Pat Roberts, who played a leading role last year in retooling the program, and House Agriculture Committee Chairman Bob Smith said the Clinton adminstration broke faith with farmers by accepting too little land.
"This is a completely inadequate effort on the administration's part," said Smith, Oregon Republican.
Roberts, a Kansas Republican, said Glickman should order enrollment of "the remaining six million authorized CRP acres as quickly as possible."
Annual rent on the new land will average $39 an acre, down from $50 now.
Agriculture Department officials said about one million to 1.5 million acres of land planted with corn, wheat and soybeans would return to production, a fairly nominal amount.
The Plains states and the Corn Belt would continue to dominate the Conservation Reserve under the new enrollment.

North Dakota would become the top state for Conservation Reserve enrollment with a total of 3.35 million acres, including two million accepted this fall. Texas, now the largest state, probably would drop to No. 2.

Enrollment fell in the upper Midwest. Minnesota would drop to 791,824 acres from 1.56 million. Iowa, with 1.74 million acres, would drop to 1.29 million acres. Michigan and Wisconsin each would decline by about 100,000 acres.
